## P-values {#sec-p-values}

```{r}
#| label: setup-3-2
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")

# z statistics from earlier examples, rounded as in those examples
two_prop_z <- function(x1, n1, x2, n2) {
  p1 <- x1 / n1; p2 <- x2 / n2
  pbar <- round((x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2), 4)
  se0 <- round(sqrt(pbar * (1 - pbar) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2)), 4)
  round((p1 - p2) / se0, 3)
}
z_debt  <- two_prop_z(171, 300, 165, 250)    # Example 3.1.1, H1: p1 != p2
z_brand <- two_prop_z(58, 200, 36, 180)      # Your Turn 3.1.1, H1: pA > pB
z_wage  <- round((358.4 - 380) / 10, 3)      # Example 2.1.1, H1: mu < 380
z_card  <- two_prop_z(84, 240, 96, 240)      # Exercise 3.1.2, H1: p1 < p2
z_grad  <- round((160 / 250 - 0.70) / round(sqrt(0.70 * 0.30 / 250), 4), 3)  # Your Turn 2.3.1, H1: p != 0.70
t_debt  <- round((184500 - 170000) / round(41200 / sqrt(20), 4), 3)            # Exercise 2.2.1, H1: mu > 170000
chi_pork <- 42.75                                                              # Your Turn 2.4.2, H1: sigma^2 != 9
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Make the decision of a test with the p-value.
2. Write the decision and the interpretation of a test from its p-value.
3. See that the p-value and the critical region give the same decision.

### Concept

So far we have decided by checking whether the test statistic falls in the
**critical region**. A second way, used by all statistical software, is the
**p-value**.

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## p-value

The **p-value** is the probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of getting a test
statistic at least as extreme as the one we observed, in the direction(s) of $H_1$.

A small p-value means our sample would be unusual if $H_0$ were true.

**Decision rule:** reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$; accept $H_0$ if p-value $\ge \alpha$.
:::

The p-value is an **area beyond the test statistic**, in the direction of $H_1$:

| $H_1$ | p-value |
|:---:|:---|
| $<$ | area to the **left** of the test statistic |
| $>$ | area to the **right** of the test statistic |
| $\ne$ | **twice** the area beyond the test statistic in one tail |

```{r}
#| label: fig-pval-z
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-cap: "The p-value as an area under the z curve (orange)"
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Left-sided"
#|   - "Right-sided"
#|   - "Two-sided"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 3.3
pval_plot(-1.5, "left", "z")
pval_plot(1.5, "right", "z")
pval_plot(1.5, "two", "z")
```

The critical-region method and the p-value method always give the **same
decision**: $z_{\text{cal}}$ falls in the critical region exactly when the
p-value is less than $\alpha$.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## What the p-value is not

The p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true. It is calculated
assuming $H_0$ is true.
:::

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-2
e <- pz_table(z_debt, "two")
```

### Example

**Example 3.2.1.** In Example 3.1.1 (household debt, urban vs rural) we
tested $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ against $H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$ and found
$z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_debt, 3)`$. The p-value of this test is
`r fmt(e$p, 4)`. Make the decision at $\alpha$ = 0.05 and compare it with the
critical-region method.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

The test is two-sided, so the p-value is the area in **both** tails beyond
$\pm`r fmt(abs(z_debt), 3)`$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-3-2
#| fig-cap: "p-value for Example 3.2.1: the two tails beyond ±2.153"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
pval_plot(z_debt, "two", "z")
```

**Where does `r fmt(e$p, 4)` come from?** (shown for illustration only; in this
course p-values are given or read from R output.) From Table 4,
$P(Z \le `r fmt(e$a, 2)`) = `r fmt(e$F, 4)`$, so one tail is
$1 - `r fmt(e$F, 4)` = `r fmt(e$tail, 4)`$, and for a two-sided test
$$
\text{p-value} = 2(`r fmt(e$tail, 4)`) = `r fmt(e$p, 4)`.
$$

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ $\quad H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.** $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_debt, 3)`$ (from Example 3.1.1)

**Step 4: p-value.** p-value = `r fmt(e$p, 4)`

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(e$p, 4)` < $\alpha$ =
0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, the proportion of households with debt is
different in urban and rural areas at the 0.05 level of significance; since
$\hat{p}_1 < \hat{p}_2$, the proportion is lower in urban areas.

| Method | Comparison | Decision |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Critical region (Example 3.1.1) | $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_debt, 3)` < `r fmt(-crit_z(.975), 3)`$ | reject $H_0$ |
| p-value | p-value = `r fmt(e$p, 4)` < 0.05 | reject $H_0$ |

Both methods give the same decision, and the interpretation is written in the
same way.
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-3-2
y1 <- pz_table(z_brand, "right")$p
y2 <- pz_table(z_grad, "two")$p
y3 <- pz_table(z_card, "left")$p
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 3.2.1

Each test was done earlier with the critical region. Use the p-value to write
the decision and the interpretation at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

(a) Your Turn 3.1.1 (brand switching): $H_0: p_A = p_B$, $H_1: p_A > p_B$, p-value = `r fmt(y1, 4)`.
(b) Your Turn 2.3.1 (graduate jobs): $H_0: p = 0.70$, $H_1: p \ne 0.70$, $\hat{p}$ = 0.64, p-value = `r fmt(y2, 4)`.
(c) Exercise 3.1.2 (price displays): $H_0: p_1 = p_2$, $H_1: p_1 < p_2$, p-value = `r fmt(y3, 4)`.
:::

::: {.workspace lines="12"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.2.1"}
(a) p-value = `r fmt(y1, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is,
the proportion of customers who switched is higher for Brand A than for Brand B
at the 0.05 level of significance.

(b) p-value = `r fmt(y2, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is,
the proportion of graduates who find a job within six months is different from
0.70 at the 0.05 level of significance; since $\hat{p}$ = 0.64, the proportion
is lower than 0.70.

(c) p-value = `r fmt(y3, 4)` $\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept $H_0$. That
is, the purchase rates with the two displays are equal at the 0.05 level of
significance.

All three decisions are the same as with the critical region.
:::

### Formula Summary

| | |
|:---|:---|
| p-value | an area beyond the test statistic, in the direction of $H_1$ (both tails for $\ne$) |
| Decision | p-value = ... [<, $\ge$] $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we [reject / accept] $H_0$. |
| Interpretation | That is, ... at the 0.05 level of significance. (reject: write $H_1$; accept: write $H_0$; two-sided reject: add the direction) |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-2-exercises
x1 <- round(pt(t_debt, 19, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)
x2 <- round(2 * pchisq(chi_pork, 19, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)
```

### Exercises

**3.2.1** For each p-value, write the decision at $\alpha$ = 0.05:
(a) 0.0312, (b) 0.0500, (c) 0.1847, (d) 0.0005.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.2.1"}
(a) 0.0312 < 0.05: reject $H_0$.
(b) 0.0500 $\ge$ 0.05: accept $H_0$.
(c) 0.1847 $\ge$ 0.05: accept $H_0$.
(d) 0.0005 < 0.05: reject $H_0$.
:::

**3.2.2** Write the decision and the interpretation at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

(a) Exercise 2.2.1 (household debt in a district): $H_0: \mu = 170000$, $H_1: \mu > 170000$, p-value = `r fmt(x1, 4)`.
(b) Your Turn 2.4.2 (weekly pork price): $H_0: \sigma^2 = 9$, $H_1: \sigma^2 \ne 9$, $s$ = 4.5, p-value = `r fmt(x2, 4)`.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.2.2"}
(a) p-value = `r fmt(x1, 4)` $\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept $H_0$. That is,
the mean household debt in the district is equal to 170,000 baht at the 0.05
level of significance.

(b) p-value = `r fmt(x2, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, the
standard deviation of the weekly pork price is different from 3 baht at the 0.05
level of significance; since $s$ = 4.5, it is higher than 3 baht.
:::
